extracted_claims.text: Under Article 43, for high-risk AI systems under Annex III the provider may choose any notified body, except where the system is intended for use by law enforcement, immigration, asylum authorities or Union institutions/bodies/agencies, in which case the relevant market surveillance authority (Art. 74(8) or (9)) acts as the notified body.

Article 43 sets distinct conformity assessment procedures depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied, referencing procedures such as those in Annex VI and Annex VII.

Annex VI describes the conformity assessment procedure based on internal control, requiring the provider to verify its quality management system complies with Article 17 and to examine the technical documentation.

Annex VII sets out the conformity assessment procedure based on assessment of the quality management system and assessment of the technical documentation, including notified body access to training and trained models when necessary and after other verification means are exhausted.

Article 48 requires that where a notified body is responsible for conformity assessment, the CE marking must be followed by the notified body's identification number, affixed by the body or under its instruction, and included in relevant promotional material.

Article 46 allows a market surveillance authority to authorise, by way of derogation from Article 43 and for a limited period, the placing on the market or putting into service of specific high-risk AI systems for exceptional reasons of public security, protection of life/health, environmental protection, or protection of key industrial/infrastructural assets.

Article 31 requires notified bodies to be independent of the provider and of any other operator with an economic interest in the high-risk AI systems assessed, as well as independent of competitors of the provider.

Article 34 requires notified bodies to verify conformity of high-risk AI systems per Article 43 procedures while avoiding unnecessary burdens, considering provider size, sector, structure and system complexity, and to make documentation available to notifying authorities on request.
Article 29 sets out the application procedure for a conformity assessment body seeking notification, referencing related provider obligations under Articles 16-25.
Article 35 requires the Commission to assign a single identification number to each notified body and to publicly list notified bodies along with their identification numbers and notified activities.

A draft/consultation document (WK-1063-2026) describes that notified bodies already notified under relevant Union harmonisation legislation (per Annex I Section A), and assessed against Article 31(4),(5),(10),(11), have power to assess conformity of high-risk AI systems, subject to Article 28.

A Council document (COM(2025) 836) references a proposed new Annex XIV listing notified and designated organisations in the Commission's NANDO system, and amendments integrating AI Act high-risk requirements into Regulation (EU) 2018/1139.

As of December 16, 2025, the NANDO system lists 51 MDR-designated notified bodies and 19 IVDR-designated bodies, with 12 MDR and 6 IVDR designation applications pending (medical device sector, not AI-Act-specific).
Member States were required to designate national competent authorities (notifying authorities and market surveillance authorities) by 2 August 2025 and communicate them to the Commission.

Italy's Law No. 132/2025, effective 10 October 2025, designates AgID (Agency for Digital Italy) as the national notifying authority responsible for assessing, designating and notifying conformity assessment bodies, and ACN as market surveillance authority.

The European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS) has been designated as the market surveillance authority for EU institutions, bodies, offices and agencies, and is also designated as a notified body for conformity assessments of certain high-risk AI systems.
As of August 2026, there are 43 applications for AI Act Notified Body designation pending across EU member state accreditation processes, with the accreditation process typically taking 18-24 months.

As of March 2026, very few bodies have been fully designated specifically for AI Act conformity assessment; existing notified bodies under other product legislation (e.g., MDR, Machinery Regulation) can assess AI components within their existing scope, but AI-specific designation remains limited.
In March 2026, DEKRA became the first body officially accredited for AI Biometric Systems under the EU AI Act, accredited by the Dutch Accreditation Council.

For high-risk AI embedded in regulated products under Annex I (e.g., medical devices, IVDs), the application date was deferred from 2 August 2027 to 2 August 2028; for stand-alone high-risk AI systems under Annex III, the date moved from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027.
Harmonised standards (CEN/CENELEC) needed to support conformity assessment have been delayed, with the original April 2025 deadline pushed to August 2025 and further delays since.

The Digital Omnibus simplification package, proposed by the European Commission in November 2025, aims to amend the AI Act and address bottlenecks including the limited availability of designated notified bodies.

report:
# Conformity Assessment Procedures and Notified Bodies Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act establishes a two-track conformity assessment system for high-risk AI systems under Article 43, supported by detailed procedures in Annexes VI and VII, but actual designation of AI-Act-specific notified bodies remains at a very early stage. While national competent authorities were due to be designated by mid-2025, as of early-to-mid 2026 few if any notified bodies had completed full AI Act-specific designation, with DEKRA's March 2026 accreditation for AI biometric systems representing the most concrete reported milestone (low confidence).

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Procedures
Article 43 establishes distinct conformity assessment pathways depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications apply, directing providers to procedures set out in Annex VI (internal control) or Annex VII (quality management system and technical documentation assessment) (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). For Annex III high-risk systems, providers may generally choose any notified body, except where systems are intended for law enforcement, immigration, asylum, or EU institutional use, in which case the relevant market surveillance authority under Article 74(8)/(9) performs the notified body function (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Annex VI requires providers to verify their own quality management system complies with Article 17 and examine technical documentation internally, without third-party involvement (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-6)). Annex VII, by contrast, requires notified body assessment of both the quality management system and technical documentation, including potential access to training and trained models as a last resort (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7)). Article 46 permits market surveillance authorities to derogate from Article 43 for a limited period on exceptional public security, health, environmental, or critical infrastructure grounds (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)). Where a notified body is involved, Article 48 requires its identification number to accompany the CE marking (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-48); [ComplianceGate](https://www.compliancegate.com/eu-artificial-intelligence-act)).

### Notified Body Requirements and Designation Process
Notified bodies must be independent of providers, other economic operators, and competitors (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-31)), and must conduct assessments proportionately to provider size and complexity while retaining documentation for notifying authorities (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-34)). Article 29 sets out the application procedure for conformity assessment bodies seeking notification (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-29)). A draft Council document indicates bodies already notified under other Union harmonisation legislation may be assessed against Article 31 criteria to gain AI Act notification authority, subject to Article 28 (medium confidence) ([Council document WK-1063-2026](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/WK-1063-2026-INIT/en/pdf)). A separate Council document references a proposed new Annex XIV listing notified bodies in the Commission's NANDO system (medium confidence) ([COM(2025) 836](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-15708-2025-INIT/en/pdf)).

### Current Designation Status
Member States were required to designate notifying authorities and market surveillance authorities by 2 August 2025 (medium confidence) ([artificialintelligenceact.eu](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/implementation-timeline); [DLA Piper](https://www.dlapiper.com/en/insights/publications/2025/08/latest-wave-of-obligations-under-the-eu-ai-act-take-effect)). Italy designated AgID as notifying authority and ACN as market surveillance authority effective October 2025 (medium confidence) ([artificialintelligenceact.eu](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/national-implementation-plans); [Studio Legale Stefanelli](https://www.studiolegalestefanelli.it/en/insights/italy-ai-act-implementing-decree)). As of August 2026, reports indicate roughly 43 pending applications for AI Act notified body designation, with accreditation processes taking 18–24 months (low confidence) ([Think Different](https://www.thinkdifferent.blog/blog/nobody-is-ready-to-certify-europe-s-ai)). DEKRA reportedly became the first body accredited for AI biometric systems in March 2026 via the Dutch Accreditation Council (low confidence, though corroborated by multiple industry sources) ([DEKRA](https://www.dekra.com/en/dekra-becomes-the-first-accredited-certification-body-for-ai-biometric-systems-under-the-eu-ai-act); [PR Newswire](https://www.prnewswire.com/apac/news-releases/dekra-becomes-the-first-accredited-certification-body-for-ai-biometric-systems-under-the-eu-ai-act-302717226.html)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Sources disagree on the pace of designation: one source implies near-zero AI-Act-specific notified bodies as of March 2026, while DEKRA's accreditation announcement in the same month suggests some progress—raising ambiguity over whether "accreditation" equals formal AI Act "notification" (both low confidence) ([Think Different](https://www.thinkdifferent.blog/blog/nobody-is-ready-to-certify-europe-s-ai); [eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act)). Sources also diverge on the exact structure of the Annex III deadline delay to around December 2027, with one citing a direct postponement and another describing an interim grace-period mechanism (medium vs. low confidence) ([Taylor Wessing](https://www.taylorwessing.com/de/international-life-sciences-newsletter/life-sciences-legal-lens-vol-2/update-ai-enabled-medical-devices-and-ivds-confirmed-as-high-risk); [CSA Research Note](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-eu-ai-act-omnibus-vii-deadline-delay-20260)). The claim that the EDPS has been designated both as market surveillance authority for EU institutions and as a notified body for certain high-risk AI systems is flagged as low confidence due to weak sourcing ([artificial-intelligence-act.com](https://www.artificial-intelligence-act.com)). Similarly, the claim that Article 35 requires the Commission to assign identification numbers and publicly list notified bodies and their notified activities is flagged as low confidence due to weak sourcing ([Article 35](https://www.artificial-intelligence-act.com/Artificial_Intelligence_Act_Article_35.html)).

## Knowledge Gaps
It remains unclear how many notified bodies have achieved full, formal AI Act notification (versus mere accreditation) as of late 2026; whether the Digital Omnibus package (COM(2025) 836) has been formally adopted; and how CEN/CENELEC harmonised standards delays are affecting Article 43 implementation. The precise final timeline for high-risk AI obligations also requires clarification.

## Methodology Note
This report was produced by an automated research pipeline: web search, source classification, confidence scores computed from source authority, recency and corroboration, and an automated review against the extracted claims.

source_links.notes: Every link points to a gathered source.

citation_coverage.notes: Nearly every factual statement is followed by a markdown citation link (e.g., Article 43, Annex VI/VII, Article 46/48/31/34/29, Council documents, DEKRA, Italy designation). Only the Knowledge Gaps section lacks citations, but these are framed as open questions rather than factual claims, which is appropriate.

hallucination_check.notes: Checked all numeric and date claims against extracted claims: '2 August 2025' deadline (claim_014), Italy AgID/ACN 'effective October 2025' (claim_015), '43 pending applications' and '18–24 months' (claim_017), DEKRA 'March 2026' accreditation (claim_019), Article 43/46/48/31/34/29 descriptions (claims_001-009), WK-1063-2026 and COM(2025) 836 (claims_011-012) all match the ground truth claims. No invented facts or numbers were found. One minor imprecision: the executive summary says national competent authorities were 'due to be designated by mid-2025' rather than the exact date '2 August 2025' used elsewhere in the body (claim_014), but this is a loose paraphrase rather than a factual error.

contradiction_disclosure.notes: The report's 'Contradictions & Uncertainties' section accurately reflects the three known contradictions: (1) disagreement on pace of designation between Think Different and eyreACT/DEKRA sources, including the accreditation-vs-notification ambiguity; (2) divergent structure of the Annex III deadline delay (Taylor Wessing vs. CSA Research Note); (3) low-confidence flags on the EDPS notified-body claim and Article 35 claim. All match the 'Known Contradictions' ground truth.
